    AI Overview
    U.S. consumer prices rose 0.9% in March 2026, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.3%, the highest since May 2024, largely driven by a 21.2% surge in gasoline prices. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, rose 0.2% monthly and 2.6% year-over-year. The data indicates significant upward pressure from energy costs due to geopolitical conflict. 
    Key Inflation Metrics (March 2026) 
    • Annual CPI (Headline): 3.3%
    • Monthly CPI (Headline): 0.9%
    • Core CPI (Annual): 2.6%
    • Core CPI (Monthly): 0.2%
    • Energy Prices: +10.9% monthly 
    Key Details on Inflation 
    • Gasoline Surge: Gasoline prices recorded a 21.2% monthly jump, the largest since data collection began in 1967, contributing nearly 75% of the total monthly rise.
    • Energy Impact: While energy makes up roughly 7% of the CPI basket, its overall economic impact is closer to 15% due to its influence on other goods.
    • Core Inflation: Core CPI, which is often considered a better measure of underlying inflation, was slightly below expectations at 2.6% annually.
    • Market Impact: The high inflation reading led to a dip in consumer sentiment, reaching the lowest level in the history of the University of Michigan survey.
    • Upcoming Changes: The CPI for April 2026 is scheduled to be released on May 12, 2026, with several CPI series being rebased to December 2024=100. 
    How the CPI is Calculated 
    • The CPI is calculated by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and measures the average change over time in prices paid by consumers for a market basket of goods and services.
    • Formula: The percentage change in the CPI from one period to another represents the inflation rate.
    • Types: There are two main types of CPI calculated by the BLS:
      • CPI-U: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (most common).
      • CPI-W: Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. 
    Inflation Impact on Wages 
    • The CPI is often used to adjust wages, salaries, and pensions for inflation.
    • The CPI-W, for instance, is used to calculate the cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) for Social Security recipients.

    • View the historical CPI trends for all items since 1913 provided by the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.
    • See the current and historical CPI data (CPIAUCSL) provided by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

    AI Overview
    As of April 10, 2026, the US Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.3% over the last 12 months ending March 2026 (not seasonally adjusted), accelerating from February's 2.4% pace. Prices rose 0.9% in March alone. Core inflation, excluding volatile food and energy, rose 2.6% year-over-year. 
    Key Takeaways (March 2026 Data): 
    • Headline Inflation: 3.3% YoY.
    • Monthly Change: +0.9% in March.
    • Core Inflation: +2.6% YoY.
    • Energy Prices: Rose 12.5% over the last 12 months, with gasoline prices rising 18.9%.
    • Food Prices: Increased 2.7% annually.
    This surge, reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, suggests elevated inflation pressures compared to early 2026. The next CPI update is scheduled for May 12, 2026.

      $100 in 1990 is equivalent in purchasing power to approximately $248.85 to $250.00 today. Due to a cumulative inflation rate of roughly 150%, a dollar from 1990 is only worth about 40 cents today, meaning prices have increased 2.5 times over the past 36 years, according to in2013dollars. 
      Key 1990 vs. Today (2026) Comparisons: 
      • $100 (1990) = Approx. $248.85 - $250.00 today.
      • $500 (1990) = Approx. $1,250.13 today.
      • $1,000 (1990) = Approx. $2,500.27 today.
      • $5,000 (1990) = Approx. $12,501.34 today.
      The average inflation rate between 1990 and 2026 was approximately 2.56% - 2.58% per year.

          Types. What are the different types of consumer price index?
          About this result
          Feedback
          An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
          AI Overview
          The main types of Consumer Price Index (CPI) in the U.S. are CPI-U (All Urban Consumers) for general inflation, CPI-W (Urban Wage Earners) for indexing Social Security, and C-CPI-U (Chained CPI) for reflecting consumer substitution. Other types include specialized research series (R-CPI-E for elderly) and regional/item-specific indexes. 
          Here are the different types of CPI, their usage examples, and related price measures:
          Main Types of CPI (Bureau of Labor Statistics)
          • CPI-U (Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers): Covers ~93% of the U.S. population, including professionals, the self-employed, and the unemployed. 
            • Usage: The most cited, broadest measure of consumer inflation used to adjust income tax brackets, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), and consumer goods prices. 
          • CPI-W (Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers): 
            A subset of CPI-U covering households where at least half the income comes from clerical or wage occupations. 
            • Usage: Specifically used to calculate cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) for Social Security benefits, federal civil service retirees, and military retirees. 
          • C-CPI-U (Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers): A "chained" formula that accounts for the fact that consumers substitute cheaper items for expensive ones.
            • Usage: Used as a more accurate reflection of cost-of-living changes, often yielding a slightly lower inflation rate than CPI-U. 
          Specialized and Research CPIs
          • R-CPI-E (CPI for Americans 62 years of age and older): Experimental index measuring spending habits of elderly consumers. 
          • Core CPI (CPI less Food and Energy): An analytical measure that removes volatile food and energy prices to show long-term inflation trends. 
          • Regional/Metropolitan CPIs: Indexes for specific cities or regions, such as "CPI-U for the Northeast" or "Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim". 
          Related Price Indices (Synonyms and Alternatives)
          • Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index (PCEPI): The Federal Reserve's preferred measure, which covers a broader range of goods and services and updates weights more frequently than CPI. 
          • Producer Price Index (PPI): Measures the average change over time in the selling prices received by domestic producers for their output. 
          • Import Price Index: Measures price changes for goods bought from other countries. 
          • CPI for Industrial/Agricultural Workers (IW/AL/RL): Used in different economic contexts, particularly in other countries, to track specific labor group costs.

            Calculation. How is the consumer price index calculated?
            About this result
            Feedback
            An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
            AI Overview
            The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is calculated monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) by measuring the cost of a "market basket" of roughly 90,000 goods and services, weighted by consumer expenditure survey data. It compares the total cost of this basket today against a base period (1982-84=100) using a weighted average of price changes. 
            Key Aspects of Calculation:
            • Market Basket:
              Represents what consumers actually purchase, including food, clothing, housing, and gasoline, weighted by popularity. 
            • Data Collection:
              Prices are collected from over 23,000 retailers and 8,000 rental units across 75 urban areas. 
            • Formula:
              The core formula is:
              CPI=(Cost of Basket in Current PeriodCost of Basket in Base Period)×100CPI equals open paren the fraction with numerator Cost of Basket in Current Period and denominator Cost of Basket in Base Period end-fraction close paren cross 100
              .               
            • Weighting:
              A weighted geometric mean is primarily used, where items with higher expenditure (e.g., rent) have a greater influence on the total index than items with lower expenditure (e.g., apples). 
            Steps in the Process:
            1. Survey Expenditure: Data from thousands of consumers is gathered to determine what to include in the "basket". 
            2. Collect Prices: BLS agents collect prices for these items monthly. 
            3. Calculate Relative Changes: The current prices are compared to the base period prices. 
            4. Weight Results: Expenditure weights are applied to items. 
            5. Aggregate Index: The results are summed up to produce the final CPI-U (All Urban Consumers) or CPI-W (Wage Earners) numbers.

              Impact on Wages. How does the consumer price index affect wages and salaries?
              About this result
              Feedback
              An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
              AI Overview
              The Consumer Price Index (CPI) directly impacts wages and salaries by measuring inflation, which prompts employers to provide cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) to help employees maintain purchasing power. When CPI rises, employees often negotiate for higher pay, and some minimum wages and union contracts are indexed to automatically increase based on CPI data. 
              • Cost-of-Living Adjustments (COLA):
                Many companies use the annual percentage change in the CPI as a benchmark to determine salary raises, ensuring pay increases keep pace with the higher cost of goods and services. 
              • Automatic Increases:
                Some collective bargaining agreements (unions) and government benefit programs, such as Social Security, automatically increase pay or payments based on CPI data to counteract inflation. 
              • Minimum Wage Adjustments:
                Several states and cities, such as Los Angeles and San Francisco, explicitly link local minimum wage increases to the CPI, causing the minimum wage to rise automatically when prices increase. 
              • Real Wage Calculations:
                The CPI is used to calculate "real wages" (nominal wages adjusted for inflation). If CPI increases faster than wages, workers suffer a loss in purchasing power, even if they receive a small raise. 
              • Tax Bracket Adjustments:
                The IRS uses CPI data to adjust federal income tax brackets to prevent "bracket creep," where inflation pushes workers into higher tax rates without a true increase in purchasing power. 
              In summary, the CPI acts as a key indicator for pay negotiations and contractual salary adjustments to keep income levels relevant to the rising cost of living.

                Limitations. What are the limitations of the consumer price index?
                About this result
                Feedback
                An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
                AI Overview
                The Consumer Price Index (CPI) limitations include substitution bias (ignoring consumers switching to cheaper goods), new product bias (delayed inclusion of new items), and quality adjustments that may mismeasure true inflation. It is an average tracker that may not reflect individual or regional cost-of-living experiences. 
                Key Limitations and Examples
                • Substitution Bias:
                  When the price of beef rises, consumers may buy more chicken. Because the CPI uses a fixed basket, it overstates the cost of living by acting as if consumers are still paying for the more expensive beef. 
                • New Product Bias:
                  The fixed basket fails to include new products until long after they are introduced. For example, when high-cost computers or cell phones were first popular, they were not immediately included, failing to capture that specific price change. 
                • Quality Changes:
                  If a car's price increases by $500 but it now has a better safety feature, the CPI tries to separate the price increase (inflation) from the quality improvement. If this adjustment is inaccurate, it misrepresents the true cost change. 
                • Population Coverage:
                  The CPI-U covers urban consumers, not rural, elderly, or specific subgroups, which may lead to inaccuracy in reflecting their specific inflation experience. 
                Synonyms for CPI Limitations 
                • Shortcomings
                • Flaws
                • Biases: (e.g., substitution, new product, quality)
                • Measurement Errors: (e.g., sampling and non-sampling errors)
                What the CPI Doesn't Measure
                • It does not include income or social security taxes. 
                • It does not measure price changes for all sectors, such as investment goods.

                  A consumer price index is a statistical estimate of the level of prices of goods and services bought for consumption purposes by households. It is calculated as the weighted average price of a market basket of consumer goods and services. Changes in CPI track changes in prices over time.
                  Source: Wikipedia
                   WikipediaMoreLessDescription
                  Formula
                  = consumer price index in current period
                  = cost of market basket in current period
                  = cost of market basket in base period
